questions.qtext: An $8$-bit register contains the $2$'s complement representation of the decimal number $-48$. The processor executes an Arithmetic Shift Right ($ASR$) instruction twice sequentially on this register. What is the final decimal value stored in the register? (Provide the answer as a base-$10$ integer, including the sign if negative).
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 1)
First, find the $8$-bit $2$'s complement of $-48$.

$+48$ in binary is $00110000_{2}$.

$1$'s complement: $11001111_{2}$.

$2$'s complement (add $1$): $11010000_{2}$.

First ASR (by $1$ bit): Arithmetic shift right preserves the sign bit (the Most Significant Bit, MSB). The MSB is $1$, so a $1$ is shifted in from the left.

$$
11010000 \xrightarrow{\text { ASR } 1} 11101000
$$

Second ASR (by $1$ bit): Again, preserve the sign bit.

$$
11101000 \xrightarrow{\text { ASR } 1} 11110100
$$

Convert $11110100_{2}$ back to decimal. Since the MSB is $1$, it is a negative number.

$2$'s complement of $11110100_{2}$ is $00001011+1=00001100_{2}=12_{10}$.

Therefore, the value is $-12$. (Note: ASR by $N$ bits is mathematically equivalent to floor division by $2^{N}$. $-48/4=-12$)

questions.qtext:
Consider a machine architecture where we want to determine if it is possible to design an expanding opcode. Assume the following parameters:

  • Instruction length: $12$ bits
  • Register operand size: $3$ bits

We wish to encode the following instruction set:

  • $4$ instructions with $3$ registers
  • $255$ instructions with $1$ register
  • $16$ instructions with$ 0$ registers

Based on the context and the bit pattern capacity method for evaluating expanding opcodes, which of the following statements are CORRECT?

options.text: The first $4$ instructions (with $3$ registers) account for exactly $4 \times 2^{9}=2048$ bit patterns in the overall instruction space.
The $255$ instructions with $1$ register account for exactly $255$ bit patterns since they only utilize a single operand.
The total maximum capacity of a $12$ -bit instruction format is $2^{12}=4096$ unique bit patterns.
The proposed instruction set cannot be encoded because the total required bit patterns ($4104$) exceed the available capacity.

questions.solution:
Answer: A, C, D

Source solution 1 (score: 0)

To determine if the instruction set is possible, we calculate the total number of bit patterns consumed by the operands for each instruction format and compare it to the total available bit patterns in a $12$-bit instruction.

$\textbf{Option A is CORRECT}$: The first format requires 3 registers. Since each register is $3$ bits, the operands consume $3 \times 3=9$ bits. The 4 instructions account for the varying operand values: $4 \times 2^{3} \times 2^{3} \times 2^{3}=4 \times 2^{9}=2048$ bit patterns.

$\textbf{Option B is INCORRECT}$: When calculating consumed bit patterns, you must account for the variable operand bits. The 255 instructions with $1$ register account for $255 \times 2^{3}=2040$ bit patterns, not just $255$.

$\textbf{Option C is CORRECT}$: A 12-bit instruction can mathematically represent a maximum of $2^{12}=4096$ distinct bit patterns.

$\textbf{Option D is CORRECT}$: Let's calculate the total required bit patterns for all instructions combined:

  • $3$-register instructions account for: $2048$ bit patterns
  • $1$-register instructions account for: $2040$ bit patterns
  • $0$-register instructions account for: $16$ bit patterns


In total, we need $2048+2040+16=\mathbf{4 1 0 4}$ bit patterns.

Because the required bit patterns ($4104$) is greater than what we have available ($4096$), it is not possible to design this instruction set with only $12$ bits.

questions.qtext: Consider an $8$-bit microprocessor with a $16$-bit address bus. An address decoder selects a specific memory block when the top three address bits ($A_{15}, A_{14}, A_{13}$) are set to $101_{2}$. The remaining $13$ bits $(x)$ are used to address individual locations within this memory block, forming the address pattern $101xxxxxxxxxxxxx_{2}$. Which of the following statements are $\textbf{TRUE}$ regarding this memory configuration? (Select all that apply)

options.text: The lowest accessible address in this memory block is $A000_{16}$.
The highest accessible address in this memory block is $\mathrm{BFFF}_{16}$.
The total size of this specific memory block is $8$ KB.
Decoding the top three address lines divides the entire $16$-bit address space into exactly $4$ independent blocks.

questions.solution:
Answer: A, B, C

Source solution 1 (score: 0)
$\textbf{Statement A is True}$: The lowest address occurs when all the 'don't care' bits ( $x$ ) are 0.

$$
1010000000000000_{2}
$$

Converting to hexadecimal (groups of 4 bits): $1010=A, 0000=0,0000=0,0000=0$. So, the lowest address is $A 000_{16}$.

$\textbf{Statement B is True}$: The highest address occurs when all the 'don't care' bits ( $x$ ) are 1.

$$
1011111111111111_{2}
$$

Converting to hexadecimal: $1011={B}, 1111={F}, 1111={F}, 1111={F}$. So, the highest address is ${BFFF}_{16}$.

$\textbf{Statement C is True}$: The size of the block is determined by the number of address lines used for locations within the block. There are $13$ bits dedicated to intra-block addressing.

$$
\text { Size }=2^{13} \text { bytes }=2^{3} \times 2^{10} \text { bytes }=8 \times 1 \mathrm{~K} \text { bytes }=8 \mathrm{~KB} .
$$

Alternatively, the total address space is $2^{16}=64 \mathrm{~KB}$. Since 3 bits are used for decoding, the space is divided by $2^{3}=8.64 \mathrm{~KB} / 8=8 \mathrm{~KB}$.

$\textbf{Statement D is False}$: Decoding 3 address lines ( $A_{15}, A_{14}, A_{13}$ ) divides the total address space into $2^{3}=8$ independent blocks, not $4$.

questions.qtext: A $16$-bit microprocessor addresses a $32$ KB block of ROM mapped contiguously starting from the base memory address $0000_{16}$. The $32$ KB ROM block is constructed using four separate $8$ KB memory chips (designated Chip $0$, Chip $1$, Chip $2$, and Chip $3$). Which of the following statements regarding the memory interfacing and addressing of this system are $\textbf{TRUE}$? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Each $8$ KB memory chip requires exactly $13$ address lines ($A_{0}$ to $A_{12}$) from the processor to select a specific byte within the chip.
The valid memory address range serviced by the third chip (Chip $2$) is exactly $4000_{16}$ to $5FFF_{16}$.

To properly decode and select exactly one of the four 8 KB chips during a memory access within the 32 KB block, address lines $A_{13}$ and $A_{14}$ can be connected to the select inputs of a 2-to-4 decoder.
During any valid memory access to this $32$ KB ROM block, the highest order address bit ($A_{15}$) must be at a logic '$1$' state.

questions.solution:
Answer: A, B, C

Source solution 1 (score: 1)

$\textbf{Statement A is True}$:The capacity of each chip is $8$ KB, which equals $8 \times 1024=8192$ bytes. Since $8192=2^{13}$, exactly $13$ address lines ($A_{0}$ through $A_{12}$) are needed to uniquely address each byte within a single chip.

$\textbf{Statement B is True}$: Based on the decoding logic from Statement C:

  • Chip $0\left(A_{14} A_{13}=00\right)$ : $0000_{16}$ to $1^{2} \mathrm{FF}_{16}$
  • Chip $1\left(A_{14} A_{13}=01\right): 2000_{16}$ to $3 \mathrm{FFF}_{16}$
  • Chip $2\left(A_{14} A_{13}=10\right)$ : $4000_{16}$ to $5 \mathrm{FFF}_{16}$
  • Chip $3\left(A_{14} A_{13}=11\right): 6000_{16}$ to $7_{57 F}{ }_{16}$


$\textbf{Statement C is True}$: The entire $32$ KB block requires $32 \times 1024=32768=2^{15}$ bytes, utilizing $A_{0}$ through $A_{14}$. The lower $13$ bits ($A_{0}$ to $A_{12}$) go directly to the chips. The next two bits ($A_{13}$ and $A_{14}$) divide the $32$ KB space into four $8$ KB segments. Using a $2$-to-$4$ decoder on $A_{13}$ and $A_{14}$ perfectly generates the four separate Chip Select $(\overline{CS})$ signals.


$\textbf{Statement D is False}$: The $32$ KB block is mapped starting at $0000_{16}$ and ends at $7FFF_{16}$. In binary, $7FFF_{16}$ is $0111111111111111_{2}$. Throughout this entire range, the most significant bit ($A_{15}$) is strictly '$0$', not '$1$'.
